items.label: a carved slab you can carry

config.why: Settled life can accumulate things: ceramics, specialists and monuments organised beyond the family. And the climate wrote itself into the art — the Running horned woman's green savanna is now the dead centre of the Sahara.

statements.s: The Great Hall of the Bulls shows observed anatomy, overlapping perspective and pigments engineered to last millennia.
statements.why: Analysis shows prepared surfaces, mixed pigments with binders, blown sprays and scaffolding marks high on the walls.

statements.s: The makers were modern humans with the same brains as you.
statements.why: Simplicity is a style choice, not a stage of intelligence.

statements.s: Simple outlines prove a primitive stage of intelligence.
statements.why: The camelid sacrum turns a pelvis into a dog by reading the bone's own shape — hard problems, solved with the materials at hand.
It takes skill, patience and social surplus — the Liangzhu cong converts time and skill into value.

activities.anchor: cave painters just drew with their hands using charcoal
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the 'child with a crayon' account
activities.name: gphCrayonSpot

config.prompt: This account of prehistoric technique contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The pigments are ground minerals: charcoal and manganese for black, ochre for red and yellow.
Pigment was mixed with binders such as animal fat, blood or plant juice.
Cave painters worked freehand in daylight at the cave mouth, like a child with a crayon.
At Lascaux some pigment was blown through tubes or directly by mouth, leaving spray effects.
The Lapita makers stamped wet clay with small toothed combs — dentate stamping.
config.correction: Deep caves were worked by stone-lamp light, hundreds of metres underground — with prepared surfaces, stencilled hands and scaffolding marks high on the walls.
config.why: This is a trained technology, learned and transmitted, with division of labour between pigment-makers and painters — the opposite of improvised doodling.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — a sarsen in kilograms
activities.name: gphSarsenEstimate

config.prompt: Stonehenge's sarsen stones weigh up to about 25 tonnes each. Roughly how many kilograms is that?
config.why: 1 tonne = 1,000 kg, so 25 tonnes ≈ 25,000 kg — stones dressed with stone hammers, dragged on sledges and rollers, with some bluestones hauled roughly 150 miles from Wales.
config.context: Between the Apollo 11 stones and Stonehenge, twenty-four millennia pass — every dynasty you have ever heard of fits in the final tenth of the timeline.

activities.caption: rebuild the argument sequence — why did they make it?
activities.name: gphTheoriesOrder

config.prompt: The readings arrived in sequence — put them in order:
items: Art for art's sake — the oldest view: people decorate; it is pleasure
Hunting and sympathetic magic — Breuil: painting an animal is a ritual act that helps capture it
Structuralism — Leroi-Gourhan maps whole cave systems: images composed by rules, not accident
Shamanism and neuropsychology — Lewis-Williams: entoptic geometric signs from trance
config.why: Each reading explains more evidence than the last — geometry, animals and location together — and the strongest current one still remains a hypothesis, unprovable for any specific cave.

activities.anchor: archaeologists have proved the cave paintings
activities.caption: run the publication — one new panel, three readings
activities.name: gphReadingBranch

config.root: A new deep-cave panel is found: geometric signs — dots, grids, zigzags — beside animal figures. Your interpretation leads the publication.

choices.label: Hunting magic — paint the hunt, get the hunt
choices.feedback: The famous theory. Check its evidence.

choices.label: Art for art's sake — decoration, pleasure
choices.feedback: The oldest view on the shelf.

hunt.text: Circumstantial only: many painted species were not staple foods, some images sit where no hunter would need them, and the geometric signs fit no hunting logic at all.

trance.text: The strongest current model: entoptic geometric patterns match what the human visual system produces in trance, and deep caves were stages for ritual specialists — it explains the most evidence and remains unprovable.

pleasure.text: It fits the beauty of the works but not the setting: who paints masterpieces in freezing, dangerous caves that no one lives in?

config.why: State the theory, name the evidence for it, and name what would have to be true for it to be wrong — the skill the syllabus actually wants.

activities.anchor: Lascaux is its defining cautionary tale
activities.caption: drag the divider — Lascaux, discovery to closure
activities.name: gphLascauxCompare

config.prompt: One cave, two eras — drag between discovery and closure:

before.text: Opened to tourists after its 1940 discovery — more than a thousand visitors a day, whose breath and lighting triggered moulds and calcium deposits: 'la maladie blanche'.

after.label: 1963–today
after.text: Closed for good in 1963; even researchers enter rarely, under strict climate control, and visitors see full-scale replicas.

config.why: Prehistoric art survives by exact accident — the sealed, stable climate of a deep cave. The moment of discovery is also the moment the clock starts running.
